meta.title: Who originally recorded "Kingston Town"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not UB40. Lord Creator’s original was recorded in 1969 and released in 1970 on Clancy Eccles’ Clandisc label. UB40’s No. 4 hit came in 1990.
meta.ogDescription: Not UB40. Lord Creator’s Clandisc original was released in 1970. UB40’s Labour of Love II cover reached No. 4 in the UK in 1990.

answer.label: Not a UB40 original — a 1970 Lord Creator single on Clandisc
answer.originalArtistDates: 1935-2023 · Trinidadian-born Jamaican calypso, ska and rocksteady singer
answer.sourceLine: UB40’s 1990 ballad is so completely theirs in the popular ear that most listeners assume they wrote and first cut it. They did neither. “Kingston Town” was written by Kentrick Patrick — who performed as Lord Creator — and first recorded by him in 1963, as a ska side titled “Babylon.” He re-cut it as reggae for producer Clancy Eccles in 1969, and that version was issued in 1970, under the title it is known by, as a single on Eccles’ Clandisc label with The Fabulous Flames’ “Holly Holy” on the flip. Creator had already largely dropped out of the music business by the 1970s; UB40’s cover, cut in 1989, revived his career and finally paid him.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Clandisc
original.released: Recorded in 1969 for producer Clancy Eccles and issued in 1970 as a 7-inch single on Eccles’ Clandisc label, coupled with “Holly Holy” by The Fabulous Flames.
original.charted: No chart position on record. It was a Jamaican-market single and never appeared on the UK or US charts; the chart life of the song belongs entirely to UB40’s cover.
original.cover: UB40, recorded 1989 and released 19 March 1990 on DEP International / Virgin as the second single from Labour of Love II. No. 4 in the UK; No. 1 in France and the Netherlands.
trail: The song’s Wikipedia entry ↗ records it as a 1970 Lord Creator single on the Clandisc label, produced by Clancy Eccles and written by Kentrick Patrick, with UB40’s cover recorded in 1989 and released on 19 March 1990.

MusicBrainz ↗ ties the recording to a 1970 Jamaican release titled “Kingston Town / Holly Holy,” credited to Lord Creator and The Fabulous Flames — though Wikipedia’s infobox renders the B-side “Holly Holly.”
The Jamaica Gleaner ↗ traces the composition back further still, to a 1963 ska recording Creator made for Vincent “Randy” Chin under the title “Babylon.”

Dancehallmag’s 2023 obituary ↗ dates the Eccles recording to 1970, and describes the European royalties the UB40 cover generated and the ownership dispute that followed — Eccles claiming fifty per cent on the strength of some of the words, Creator maintaining he wrote the whole thing.

authors.name: Lord Creator
authors.kicker: Wrote it and recorded it first
authors.heading: Lord Creator
authors.metaLine: Kentrick Randolph Patrick, 1935-2023 · born San Fernando, Trinidad · moved to Jamaica 1959
authors.bio: Kentrick Randolph Patrick was born in San Fernando, Trinidad in 1935 and moved to Jamaica in late 1959, arriving just in time to become one of the foundational voices of the island’s recording industry. His 1962 “Independent Jamaica” was chosen to mark the country’s independence and was the first record issued by Chris Blackwell’s Island Records in the UK (Island 001). He is also the song’s credited writer — the composition credit reads Kentrick Patrick, his legal name, so the writer and the first performer are one man listed under two names on two sets of paperwork. He brought the song with him from Trinidad and first cut it in 1963 for Vincent “Randy” Chin under a different title. By the 1970s he had largely dropped out of the business; UB40’s cover of “Kingston Town” brought him back, and Jamaica awarded him the Order of Distinction in 2022. He died on 30 June 2023, aged 87.

authors.name: UB40
authors.heading: UB40
authors.metaLine: British reggae band, formed Birmingham 1978 · cover released 19 March 1990
authors.bio: UB40’s “Kingston Town” was recorded in 1989 and released on 19 March 1990 as the second single from Labour of Love II, on DEP International through Virgin. It reached No. 4 in the UK and No. 1 in France and the Netherlands, and remains the band’s signature ballad. The band never hid the song’s origin — the whole Labour of Love project was openly a covers series — but the arrangement is so identified with them that the authorship gets forgotten. It was certified Platinum in the UK in March 2023 ↗, after more than 600,000 units.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong originator
misattribution.intro: The belief is chronological, not malicious — UB40 credited the writer all along. Here is what the record actually shows.

items.why: Their 1990 recording is the version almost everyone has heard, and it is treated as the song’s starting point.
Recorded in 1969 with producer Clancy Eccles and issued in 1970 as a single on Eccles’ Clandisc label, backed with The Fabulous Flames’ “Holly Holy.”
Kentrick Patrick is Lord Creator’s legal name — the writer and the first performer are the same man.
Creator first cut the composition as a ska side for Vincent “Randy” Chin in 1963 under the title “Babylon”; the 1970 Eccles session reworked it around Kingston and gave it the title it is known by.
Press reports of a claim over “Stars Are Blind” named UB40 as the party suing; the band later said that was incorrect.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Kentrick Patrick and first recorded by him, as Lord Creator, in 1963 under the title “Babylon”; re-cut for Clancy Eccles and released in 1970 on Clandisc as “Kingston Town.” UB40’s version came out on 19 March 1990.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: A record can be famous in Jamaica and invisible everywhere else, and in 1970 that gap was almost total. Lord Creator’s “Kingston Town” was a Jamaican single on a Jamaican producer’s label with a Jamaican pressing run; no British or American chart ever registered it. UB40’s version arrived twenty years later through a major-label pipeline, in a decade when a polished reggae ballad could go to No. 1 across Europe.

The other reason is that Labour of Love II was designed to do exactly this. UB40 built the series to re-cut reggae records they loved, and the arrangements are lush enough to feel authored rather than borrowed. The band were never coy about the source — the credit is on the sleeve — but a No. 4 hit heard by millions overwrites a single heard by thousands.
detailsBody: 1963 — Lord Creator records the composition for producer Vincent “Randy” Chin as a ska side under a different title, “Babylon.”
1969 — producer Clancy Eccles has him re-record it as a reggae side, reworked to be about Kingston.
1970 — issued as a single on Eccles’ Clandisc label, backed with The Fabulous Flames’ “Holly Holy.”
1989 — UB40 record their version for Labour of Love II.
19 March 1990 — UB40’s single is released on DEP International; it reaches No. 4 in the UK and No. 1 in France and the Netherlands.

1990s — with the European royalties flowing, Clancy Eccles claims fifty per cent of the song on the strength of having written some of the words; Creator maintains he wrote the whole thing, and says the publishers agreed after investigating.
2007 — the composition’s copyright holders pursue a claim over Paris Hilton’s “Stars Are Blind”; press reports name UB40 as the suing party, which the band later says was incorrect.
2022 — Jamaica awards Lord Creator the Order of Distinction (Officer). He dies on 30 June 2023.
context.pull: The credit was always on the sleeve. Nobody read the sleeve.

schema.faqAnswer: No. "Kingston Town" was written by Kentrick Patrick, who performed as Lord Creator, and first recorded by him — in 1963 as "Babylon," then re-cut for producer Clancy Eccles in 1969 and released in 1970 on Clandisc under the title "Kingston Town." UB40's 1990 version is a cover.
